description.text: How net external force, mass, and acceleration are related for a constant-mass system.

objectives.statement: Define a system, external force, net external force, mass, and acceleration.
State Newton’s second law in words and as F_net = m a for constant mass.
Calculate acceleration from net external force and mass in a simple one-dimensional situation.

text.text: This lesson treats a chosen system with constant mass in an inertial frame. We use the net external force and focus on simple one-dimensional situations. Variable-mass systems, rotation, non-inertial frames, and full two-dimensional vector resolution are outside this lesson.

definition.text: The object or group of objects chosen for analysis.
The vector sum of all external forces acting on the chosen system. It is the overall unbalanced external force, so direction matters.

text.text: Mass measures inertia and is measured in kilograms. Weight is a gravitational force and is measured in newtons. They are not the same quantity.

statement.text: For constant mass, acceleration is directly proportional to the net external force, inversely proportional to mass, and points in the direction of the net external force.

conditions.text: Use this form in a classical inertial frame with constant mass.

caption.text: Net external force equals mass multiplied by acceleration.

conditions.text: For calculation, rearrange as a = F_net / m.

prompt.text: A 5.0 kg crate experiences a net horizontal external force of 20 N to the right. Find its acceleration.

steps.description: Use the rearranged form of Newton’s second law.
Substitute the net force and mass.
The direction follows the direction of the net force.

answer.text: The crate accelerates at 4.0 m/s^2 to the right.

items.text: Identify the external forces and combine them to obtain F_net.
Use a = F_net / m and include the direction.
Check the units and whether the result agrees with the force and mass changes.

points.text: Use the net external force, not one force chosen in isolation.
F_net = m a and a = F_net / m for constant mass.
If F_net is zero, acceleration is zero in the stated direction.

prompt.text: Which force should be used in F_net = m a?

content.text: The vector sum of all external forces on the chosen system

feedback.text: Newton’s second law uses the net external force: the vector sum of the external forces on the chosen system.

prompt.text: A 2.0 kg object has a net force of 10 N east. What is its acceleration?

feedback.text: a = F_net / m = 10 N / 2.0 kg = 5.0 m/s^2, in the direction of the net force: east.

hint.text: Divide force by mass, then keep the force direction.

prompt.text: Can forces act on an object while its acceleration is zero?

content.text: Yes, if the external forces balance so F_net = 0
No, any force always causes acceleration

feedback.text: Yes. Individual forces may be present, but balanced forces give zero net force and therefore zero acceleration.

claim.text: Mass and weight are the same thing.

correction.text: Mass measures inertia in kilograms; weight is a gravitational force in newtons.

claim.text: The largest force acting on an object determines its acceleration.

correction.text: Acceleration is determined by the vector sum of all external forces: the net external force.

summary.text: Choose a system and find its net external force.
Use F_net = m a, or a = F_net / m.
Acceleration has the direction of F_net.
